analysis.one_liner: Caps student loan payments at ten percent of income, forgives remaining balances after ten years, and refinances private loans.
analysis.headline: The bill had 55 House sponsors and cosponsors, all Democrats, and died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let federal student loan borrowers cap their monthly payments at 10% of any income they earn above 150% of the poverty line, and would have forgiven whatever was still owed after 120 monthly payments — counting the 10 years before the bill as time already served. It would have capped interest on new federal loans at 3.4%, let certain private student loan borrowers refinance into federal loans at 3.4%, required private lenders to sell those loans to the Education Department when asked, paused interest during up to three years of unemployment, cut the public-service forgiveness waiting period in half, and made forgiven debt tax-free.
analysis.who_benefits: Student loan borrowers, especially those with high debt relative to income. Someone earning a modest salary would pay at most a tenth of their income above the poverty line each month, and after ten years of payments (or ten years of documented hardship) the remaining balance would be wiped out tax-free. Borrowers stuck with high-rate private loans whose debt exceeded their income could refinance into a 3.4% federal loan. Unemployed borrowers would get up to three years without interest piling up. Public-service workers would see their loans forgiven after five years instead of ten, and primary care doctors in underserved areas would newly qualify.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Student loan borrowers with high debt

how_it_helps.text: Caps monthly federal loan payments at one-twelfth of 10% of the borrower's income above 150% of the federal poverty line, with $0 payments during documented economic hardship.

Forgives the remaining loan balance after 120 monthly payments, counting the ten years before enactment and months of economic-hardship deferment toward that total, and excludes the forgiven amount from taxable income.
Caps the interest rate on all new federal Direct Loans at 3.4%.

Lets borrowers with high private student loan debt relative to their income consolidate those private loans into a federal Direct Consolidation Loan at 3.4%, and directs the consumer bureau to write rules requiring private lenders to sell eligible loans to the Secretary of Education for that purpose.
Has the Secretary of Education pay the interest on unsubsidized federal loans during up to three years of unemployment deferment, so interest does not compound while a borrower is out of work.
Cuts the Public Service Loan Forgiveness requirement from 120 payments to 60 and adds primary care physicians in federally designated underserved areas as eligible.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would cover the cost of forgiveness, the 3.4% rate cap, and the interest subsidy — the Congressional Budget Office never scored the bill because it never got that far. Private student lenders would also give up future interest revenue when the government bought their loans at principal plus accrued interest. An honest supporter would also concede that easier forgiveness can feed back into tuition: schools face less pressure to hold costs down if students can borrow more with less fear of repayment.

drawbacks.text: The cost to the Treasury would have been large: forgiveness after ten years for tens of millions of existing borrowers, a below-market 3.4% rate on new loans, and three years of interest paid by the government during unemployment are all federal spending, and the bill was never scored because no committee ever considered it.

The forgiveness program was retroactive — it credited payments and hardship deferments going back ten years before enactment — so a substantial share of the benefit would have gone out immediately rather than gradually, adding to the fiscal cost.
Broad, predictable forgiveness can encourage more borrowing and give colleges room to keep raising tuition, since someone other than the student ultimately absorbs the unpaid balance.

The private-loan refinancing door was open only for one year after enactment and only to borrowers whose income was at or below their total education debt, leaving out many private-loan borrowers who were struggling but did not meet that test.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers drowning in student debt, the bill offered real, immediate relief: capped payments, a ten-year exit ramp, and a way out of high-rate private loans. The honest trade-off is that this relief is a federal expenditure — the government eats the unpaid balances — and cheap, forgiving credit can contribute to the tuition inflation that created the debt problem in the first place. A well-designed version would have paired relief with cost controls on colleges; this bill did not, but the underlying problem it addressed — more than $1 trillion in student debt impeding homeownership, saving, and business formation — was real and, as the bill's own findings stated, growing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees in March 2013 and sent to an education subcommittee a month later, and no committee ever held a markup or brought it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Karen Bass introduced the Student Loan Fairness Act on March 21, 2013, with 34 original cosponsors joining on introduction day.

The bill was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and also to the Financial Services and Ways and Means Committees, and on April 23, 2013 it was referred to the Higher Education and Workforce Training subcommittee.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.
All 55 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; not a single Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders and loan servicers kept their existing high-rate loans, accrued interest, and fees untouched, while the roughly $1 trillion borrower debt load the bill targeted stayed exactly as it was. Taxpayers avoided the cost, but the borrowers the bill was written for got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private lenders and servicers; borrowers got nothing

industries.industry: Private student lenders (e.g., Sallie Mae and other consumer lenders)
industries.note: The bill would have let borrowers hand their high-rate private loans to the Education Department for 3.4% refinancing and would have required lenders to sell those loans at principal plus accrued interest when asked. That converts future interest revenue the lender had locked in into a one-time payoff, and it removes the high-rate loans from their books.

industries.industry: Legacy FFEL lenders and guaranty agencies
industries.note: Forgiveness after ten years, the 3.4% rate cap, and interest paid by the Secretary during hardship would cut the interest income and federal subsidy payments on the federal-guaranteed loans these lenders still hold.

Mass consolidation of private loans into federal loans would shift large volumes of servicing from private-lender operations to Department of Education contractors, and lower balances and faster forgiveness mean smaller servicing revenue over time — though the servicer industry as a whole might still win the new federal contracts.
